title: Statement of Michael Eugenis, Director of Resource Planning, Arizona Public Service Company for Panel 2 Reliability in the West Under Drought Conditions re FERC's 10/21/2026 Reliability Technical Conference under AD26-8.

documents.name: Statement of Michael Eugenis.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



       Reliability Technical Conference     )      Docket No. AD26-8-000
                                            )


                             Statement of Michael Eugenis
                 Director of Resource Planning, Arizona Public Service
                Wednesday, October 21, 2026 – Technical Conference
               Panel 2: Reliability in the West Under Drought Conditions


       Good afternoon, I am Michael Eugenis, Director of Resource Planning at Arizona Public

Service (“APS”). I would like to thank the Commission for the opportunity to participate in

today’s conference and discuss APS’s approach to maintaining reliability in the West under

drought conditions.


       I began my career with APS as an Engineer in the Transmission and Distribution (T&D)

organization and subsequently held positions of increasing responsibility in Customer

Construction, Transmission Planning, and System Protection. In 2021, I transitioned to

Resource Management as Supervisor of Resource Planning, became a manager in 2022, and

was promoted to Director of Resource Planning in 2024. I have been involved in the

development of two Integrated Resource Plans (IRPs); APS’s 2023 IRP, which was filed at the

Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC) in November 2023, and the upcoming 2026 IRP, which

will be filed October 30th of this year.


       APS is Arizona’s largest electric utility, serving more than 1.5 million customers. Given

Arizona’s extreme summer conditions, APS understands the importance of maintaining

reliable generation while accounting for drought conditions impacting utilities throughout the

West. The following comments describe APS’s perspective on the topics and questions that

may be discussed during the Commission’s Reliability Technical Conference.
            APS Comments on Possible Panel Topics and Questions

1.     There are estimates that it will take 8 – 10 years of good precipitation (rain and
       snowpack) to return reservoirs to adequate levels to support the 4,500 MW of Colorado
       River hydropower production, and such precipitation levels are not expected. How are
       WECC and western utilities preparing to ensure reliability in the short-term and long-
       term for what appears to be a challenging future?

Arizona’s three largest utilities, APS, SRP, and TEP, combined have less than 200 MW of direct
reliance on power from Colorado River federal hydropower facilities such as Hoover Dam and
Glen Canyon Dam. Even so, prolonged drought can reduce regional operating flexibility and
market liquidity and create operational risk for generating facilities that depend on Colorado
River Basin water for cooling or operation.


For APS specifically, the company is a partial owner and operator of two thermal generators
that utilize Colorado River water for cooling; Four Corners Generating Station, which uses
water from a Colorado River tributary, and Sundance power plant, which uses Colorado River
water that is moved to the plant via the Central Arizona Project canal system. APS closely
monitors hydrologic conditions to assess potential impacts on the Sundance and Four Corners
generating plants and to guide facility-specific mitigation planning. At Sundance, APS has
sufficient groundwater rights and an onsite well that can provide cooling water if Colorado
River deliveries are interrupted. At Four Corners, APS monitors Navajo Reservoir operations
and potential shortage-management actions because the plant relies on reservoir water for
cooling. Navajo Reservoir has substantially less storage capacity than Lake Powell and Lake
Mead, meaning, its conditions can recover more quickly in response to favorable hydrologic
conditions. Nonetheless, APS continues to evaluate alternative water sources to supplement
the plant's water supply.


The rest of APS’s thermal generation does not use surface water, however, an increased
reliance on groundwater by municipalities and other large users that have historically utilized
Colorado River water could lead to additional drawdown of surrounding aquifers. APS has a
history of looking for innovative strategies to recycle or recapture water because of the climate
in the Southwest. For example, Palo Verde uses recycled municipal wastewater for cooling
rather than river water or groundwater, reducing its exposure to Colorado River hydrologic
conditions.


2.     How should resource adequacy planning models change in response to potential long-
       term reductions in inflows, minimum power pool constraints, and declining reservoir
       elevations that make hydropower an uncertain resource rather than a predictable
        seasonal asset? How have retirements of conventional generation combined with the
       addition of large loads affected this circumstance?

Resource adequacy studies should evaluate a range of hydrologic conditions and the resulting
effects on hydroelectric generation and regional market availability. APS uses probabilistic
and chronological planning methods to evaluate resource adequacy across multiple weather
and resource conditions. APS also evaluates stressed-system scenarios that limit import
availability to reflect potential market scarcity and reduced surplus energy from neighboring
systems during periods of regional stress. These studies must also reflect the pace and
sequence of conventional resource retirements and large-load growth. Retirements can
reduce available capacity, flexibility, and essential reliability services, while rapid large-load
growth can materially increase both peak demand and energy requirements. Scenario analysis
should therefore test accelerated load growth, including significant amounts of high load factor
load, retirement delays or advances, and potential lags in generation, transmission, and fuel-
infrastructure development.


3.     What is the most significant risk in reliability planning frameworks for the West (e.g.,
       hydrological modeling, cross-sector coordination, load forecasting, or extreme-event
       assumptions) that could undermine near and long-term reliability in the Western
       Interconnection? How significant is this risk and how can it best be mitigated?

The most significant long-term reliability risk is that load demand on the Western Interconnect
may grow faster than utilities can permit, site, finance, interconnect, and construct the
generation, fuel infrastructure, and transmission needed to reliably serve customers. Many of
these assets require years to develop, particularly high-voltage transmission infrastructure.
Delays in any part of that process could result in insufficient dependable capacity to meet
growing demand.


This risk is amplified when rapid load growth coincides with other system stresses, including
reduced water availability, constrained imports, fuel limitations, conventional resource
retirements, or delays in replacement resources and infrastructure. Mitigating these risks
requires diversified resource portfolios, dependable fuel supplies, long-term transmission
development, and resource adequacy studies that evaluate correlated system stresses rather
than individual risks in isolation.


4.     What structure is needed to enable coordinated decision making by water users and
       water rights holders (e.g., water managers, tribal nations, municipal utilities,
       agricultural users, and large industrial loads), who may not regularly interact and who
       would need to coordinate with grid operators to determine priority for health, safety
       and economic needs? How are electric system operators aligning their operational and
        market planning cycles with water management and allocation decisions by the United
       States Bureau of Reclamation and state water authorities’ timelines for water releases,
       allocations, etc. that directly affect hydropower output?

There are several existing forums in the West that are attempting to coordinate and negotiate
over this scarce resource. APS supports continued coordination among the Bureau of
Reclamation, state water agencies, tribal entities, water users, and electric utilities to improve
transparency and planning certainty. Timely access to information regarding water-
management decisions that may affect electric generation is critical.


On August 21, 2026, the Department of Interior issued the Record of Decision (“ROD”) for
the Decision Framework for Colorado River Guidelines: Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell
and Lake Mead (2027–2036), establishing a 10-year decision framework with a broad
operational range that will be used to develop future operational guidelines for Lake Powell
and Lake Mead. The ROD lays out a plan to establish operating guidelines every two years,
based on system conditions, with the possibility of those guidelines changing sooner if system
conditions threaten the Department’s infrastructure on the river. APS understands this as an
attempt to provide as much operating certainty as possible. Advance notice allows utilities to
assess operational impacts, implement mitigation measures as appropriate, and incorporate
revised assumptions into resource planning and operational decision-making.


5.     How should planners better integrate rapidly shifting hydrological forecasts into multi-
       year transmission, resource adequacy, and infrastructure planning processes, which
       traditionally assume stable water conditions?

APS uses long-term planning horizons, evaluates system performance across many years of
historical weather conditions, and employs chronological assessments to evaluate reliability
under varying system supply and demand conditions. APS also evaluates sensitivities that
limit import availability to reflect potential market scarcity and reduced surplus energy from
neighboring systems during periods of regional stress.


As weather uncertainty increases, including variability in precipitation patterns and hydrologic
conditions, regional long-term planning should incorporate updated forecasts through
thematic, weather-related scenarios and sensitivity analyses rather than rely on a single
outlook. Planners should evaluate not only the reliability impacts of changing hydrology,
including effects transmitted through neighboring systems and interregional market
conditions, but also compound events in which reduced hydropower availability coincides with
extreme heat, constrained imports, fuel limitations, generator outages, or rapid load growth.
 This integrated approach can identify correlated vulnerabilities early enough to adjust
resource, transmission, fuel, and infrastructure plans.


6.     How should WECC entities prepare for compounding reliability stress when hydropower
       shortages align with extreme heat, availability limitations for conventional generation
       resources due to cooling shortages, the retirement of conventional generation, reduced
       natural gas supplies due to limited freshwater for Gulf Coast refineries, and rapidly
       growing loads in the Southwest, creating simultaneous supply and demand pressures?
       Are there datasets that operators lack today that would improve reliability operations
       and planning in the Colorado River Basin (e.g., real time tributary inflow telemetry,
       coordinated reservoir operations data, or cross-sector demand projections)?

WECC entities should model compound events in which prolonged drought and persistently
low reservoir levels coincide with extreme heat, cooling-water constraints, conventional
generator retirements, natural-gas supply constraints, and rapid load growth. As stated
above, the ability to maintain a balanced generation portfolio is an important piece of planning
for extreme conditions in the future. For example, APS is beginning to evaluate vulnerabilities
that historically posed limited risk to resource planning, including daily fuel-delivery
limitations and pipeline transportation capacity constraints that could limit the availability of
regional gas supplies.


During prolonged high-demand conditions, these fuel constraints could reduce available
generator output and decrease regional market liquidity. Reliability assessments should test
the magnitude, duration, and timing of these conditions and determine whether available
generation and market purchases can sustain customer demand throughout the event. The
results should inform fuel-assurance measures, contracting strategies, operating procedures,
resource additions, and transmission planning before an emergency develops.


Conclusion

In summary, APS recognizes that multiple, overlapping conditions can create reliability risks
across the Western Interconnection. Addressing these risks requires utilities and regional
entities to use realistic, chronological planning methods, maintain diversified resource
portfolios, and coordinate closely with other stakeholders. Timely hydrologic information,
long-term transmission and infrastructure development, and fuel assurance will be essential
to protecting customers as conditions evolve.


Ultimately, maintaining reliable electric service in the West will depend on proactive and
coordinated planning that anticipates the interconnected effects of water availability, fuel
 supply, infrastructure development, and growing demand before those challenges become
emergencies.


                                       Respectfully submitted,


                                       /s/ Michael Eugenis

                                       Michael Eugenis
                                       Director of Resource Planning for Arizona Public
                                       Service Company


      Dated: 10/12/2026
